column2: How can you go, leaving this lotus-eyed boy, adorned with bath and garlands like a newly wedded groom?
[Bhishma said:] Hearing the jackal's piteous lament, all those men turned back then, for the sake of the boy.
[The vulture said:] "Shame! Men of little courage, spoken to by a cruel, small-minded, petty jackal, why do you turn back?
Abandoned by the five elements, empty, turned to wood, why do you grieve for a motionless thing? Why do you not grieve for yourselves?
Perform fierce austerity, by which you may be freed from sin; everything is gained by austerity; what will lamenting do?
Know that fortunes, unwished-for, come with their forms; by it this world goes, having given endless grief.
Wealth, cows, gold, jewels and gems, and offspring too, have austerity as their root and are gained through austerity.
As done among beings, so one obtains pleasure and pain; a creature is born taking up pains and pleasures.
A son does not go by his father's deed, nor a father by his son's; each goes by another way, leaving behind good and bad deeds.
Practise dharma with effort, turn back from adharma, and in due time attend to the gods and the twice-born.
Give up grief and dejection, turn back from affection for the son; let him be abandoned in the open, and then return quickly.
Whatever good deed or dreadful wrong one does, the doer alone partakes of it; what have kinsmen to do with it?
Kinsmen do not stay here having left a dear kinsman; giving up affection, they go away with eyes full of tears.
Wise or foolish, rich or poor, all go under the sway of time, bearing their good and bad.
What will you do by grieving? Why mourn the dead? For time is lord of all, impartial by dharma.
Death enters the young and the child, the old, even those in the womb; such is this world."
[The jackal said:] "Alas, affection has been dulled by the vulture here, of little wit, in you who are overcome by love of your son and grieve greatly.
With measured, well-applied words full of humility, you go off, leaving behind an affection hard to give up, on this watered ground.
Alas, from separation from a son, from living in a place empty of the dead, the sorrow of those who cry out is great, like that of cows who have lost their calves.
Today I know the grief of men on earth; seeing their piteous love, tears came to me too.
Effort must ever be made; what is made succeeds by fate; fate and human effort come together through the ender.
One should never be despondent; from despondency, where is happiness? By effort wealth is gained; why do you go, pitiless ones?
Born of your own flesh, a body made of half of your own, the founder of your fathers' line: where will you go, leaving him in the forest?
Or when the sun has set and twilight has come, you may take the boy then, or you may stay here."
[The vulture said:] "A thousand years and more have passed, men, since I was born, and I have not seen a living one, dead, woman, man or eunuch.
Some die in the womb, some die as soon as they are born, some die while still crawling, and others in youth.
Fortunes here are impermanent, even for four-footed creatures and birds; for the moving and the unmoving, life stands in front.
Parted from beloved wives and afflicted by grief for sons, burning with sorrow, they go home every day.
Thousands of unwished things and hundreds of wished ones have been left behind here, and the kinsmen go away deeply grieved.
Let this lifeless one be abandoned, empty, turned to wood; for those attached to another body worship a corpse, a log.
Why do you not leave your tears for one whose life has gone astray? This affection is useless and the keeping is useless.
He hears with neither eyes nor ears, nor sees; so leave him and go quickly to your own homes.
I have spoken with words based on the dharma of liberation, reasoned and not harsh; go quickly each to his own dwelling."
Spoken to harshly by one endowed with wisdom and knowledge, giving the name of understanding, the men turned back.
[The jackal said:] "This one, of golden hue, adorned with ornaments, how can you abandon him at a vulture's word, your son who gives the ancestors' offering?
There is no conflict in affection, in lament and weeping; but by abandoning this dead one, anguish will surely come.
It is heard that when the Shudra Shambuka was slain, a brahmana's child was revived, through dharma, by Rama of true valour.
So too the boy of the royal sage Shveta, who had met his appointed end, a dead one, was brought back to life by one constant in dharma.
So some perfected sage or even a deity may show pity to you who weep here, miserable ones."
[Bhishma said:] Thus addressed, those grieving, fond of their son, turned back; laying his head in their lap, they wept at great length.
[The vulture said:] "Wet with tears, pained by the touch of hands, by the order of the king of dharma, he has been put into a long sleep.
Even one joined to austerity is not spared at his time; this is the end of all affection, this the city of the dead.
Kinsmen, ever abandoning thousands of children and old people, remain on the ground in sorrow through days and nights.
Enough of insisting, this warding off of grief; it is not to be believed; how could he live again here today?
By the jackal's words he will not regain life; for one dead and with body cast off there is no body again.
Not by giving a form, nor by hundreds of jackals, can this boy be revived, even in hundreds of years.
Even if Rudra or Kumara or Brahma or Vishnu himself were to grant him a boon, only then might this child live.
Not by the release of tears, not by consolation, nor by long weeping will he live again here.
I, the jackal, you, and the kinsmen of this child, taking up dharma and adharma, all proceed on the road.
The unpleasant and harsh, treachery, another's wife, adharma and falsehood: the wise man should turn away from these from afar.
Seek with effort truth, dharma, the good, the just, great compassion for beings, straightness and honesty.
For those who do not look after mother and father, kinsmen and friends while they live, there is a reversal of dharma.
He who does not see with his eyes and does not stir at all, what will you do, weeping at the end of the final rites?"
[Bhishma said:] Thus addressed, leaving that son on the ground, overwhelmed with grief, burning with love for the son, the kinsmen went to their homes.
[The jackal said:] "Dreadful is this world of mortals, destroyer of all creatures; parting from loved ones and a short life.
Seeing this much falsehood and untruth, one who speaks unpleasantly in reply, rebirth increases sorrow and grief.
This human world does not please me even for a moment; alas, men, you turn back at a vulture's word.
Burning with grief for a son, as if without sense, how do you go, you who were affectionate, leaving your love for your son, having heard the words of a vulture, sinful and uncultivated?
After happiness comes sorrow, after sorrow happiness; in a world joined with pleasure and pain there is nothing here endless.
Laying this child, endowed with beauty, on the ground, where will you go, fools, abandoning a son who is the source of your family's grief?
Endowed with beauty and youth, shining as if with splendour, I see him alive in my mind; there is no doubt.
His destruction too is unfit; you men will gain happiness; for you, burnt by the fire of grief for your son, even the dead is fitting today.
Having made yourselves expect pain, and having yourselves held happiness, where will you go today, abandoning him like men of small mind?"
[Bhishma said:] So, by one whose opposition to dharma, a lover of falsehood, a dweller in the cremation ground, always seeking prey at night,
the kinsmen were brought to a middle ground by the jackal's words like nectar, for his own purpose, and stood there.
[The vulture said:] "This place is crowded with the dead, frequented by yakshas and rakshasas, a dreadful forest region, resounded by owls,
fearsome and very terrible, dark as a blue cloud; leaving the body in it, attend to the rites of the dead.
Before the sun reaches its setting and while the directions are clear, leave him and attend to the rites of the dead.
Hawks cry harshly, dreadful jackals howl, the lords of beasts roar in answer, and the sun goes to its setting.
Trees are tinged with the dark smoke of pyres, and in the cremation ground the hungry creatures rejoice.
All the very dreadful ones of mighty valour in this region, deformed eaters of flesh, will attack you.
This forest region is far, and fear will be here; abandon this thing become wood; put up with the jackal's talk.
If you hear the jackal's words, vain and false, you will all perish, with your good sense lost."
[The jackal said:] "Stay; there is nothing to fear here as long as the sun burns; so long, out of love for the son, act here without despondency.
Weep as you like, trusting; look with affection as you like; stay as long as the sun; what use are the words of a flesh-eater to you?
If, with minds bewildered, you accept the vulture's harsh and rash words, you will have no son."
[Bhishma said:] When the sun had not set, the vulture said "it has set," and the jackal said it had not; the two, hungry, spoke to the dead boy's household.
Both skilled in their own aims, king, the vulture and the jackal, wearied by hunger and thirst, spoke relying on the shastra.
Of those two, learned in knowledge, the jackal and the bird, with words like nectar, the kinsmen now stayed, now moved to go.
Overcome with grief and dejection, weeping, they stood, and were bewildered by the skill of those two who were clever in their own aims.
While those two learned ones thus disputed, to the kinsmen who stood there Shankara came.
Then the trident-bearer said to those men, "I am the giver of a boon"; they replied with these words, grieved, bowed and standing:
For all of us who have lost our only son and wish to live, you should give life by granting life to our son.
Thus addressed, the blessed one, with his hand full of water, gave life to that boy, for a hundred years.
And the blessed Pinaka-bearer, intent on the good of all beings, gave the jackal and the vulture a boon that ended their hunger.
Then, bowing to that god, filled with joy at the good, their work done, happy and delighted, they set off, lord.
By long freedom from despondency and a firm resolve, and by the grace of the god of gods, fruit is quickly gained.
See the meeting with the god and the resolve of the kinsmen; the tears of the weeping poor were wiped away.
See, too, that in a short time, by seeking resolve, the afflicted gained the grace of Shankara and found happiness.
They were astonished and delighted at their son's revival, best of the Bharatas, by the grace of Shankara.
Then, quickly, king, having heard the story born of grief, they entered the city with the son in their arms, glad at heart. This wisdom has been shown for all four classes.
Hearing this auspicious tale, joined with dharma, wealth and liberation, a man always rejoices here and hereafter.
Having reached the Himalaya, there was a great silk-cotton tree, grown through many years, with branches, trunk and leaves.
There intoxicated elephants, oppressed by heat and worn by toil, rested, mighty-armed, and other kinds of deer likewise.
That tree, of the girth of a hundred cubits, with dense shade, resounded with parrots and mynas, full of fruit and flower.
Caravans, merchants and ascetics living in the forest dwelt in that most lovely of trees as travellers on the road.
Seeing its vast branches and its trunk on every side, Narada approached it and said, bull of the Bharatas:

Oh, how lovely you are, oh, how charming; we are always pleased by you, best of trees, Shalmali.
mahabharata:12:150.8	Always birds, dear, and below deer and elephants live in you, delighted and even more charming.
mahabharata:12:150.9	Your branches, great-branched one, and your trunk are vast; I never see them broken by the wind.
mahabharata:12:150.15	Of all of these, separately and together, a sweet voice is heard, singing most charmingly at the season of flowering.
mahabharata:12:150.16	So these elephants, glad, adorning their herds, oppressed by heat, find happiness in you, Shalmali.
mahabharata:12:150.17	So also you are adorned by other kinds of deer, and by the lodgings of caravans you shine like Meru among trees.
mahabharata:12:150.18	With brahmanas, with ascetics perfected in austerity, with sages, I think your dwelling equal to heaven.
mahabharata:12:150.19	Out of kinship or friendship, Shalmali, without doubt, the terrible wind guards you everywhere, always.
mahabharata:12:150.20	You have attained the highest lowness before the wind, Shalmali, I am yours," by which the wind protects you.
I see no tree nor firm mountain on earth that has not been broken by the force of the wind; so I think.
But you, Shalmali, are surely always protected by the wind with his retinue, and for that you stand, without doubt."
[Shalmali said:] "The wind is not my friend, brahmana, nor kinsman, nor well-wisher; nor the Supreme Lord by whom the wind protects me.
My strength is such that the wind, though terrible, Narada, does not reach even an eighteenth part of my breath.
When the mighty wind came, I checked him by force, as he broke trees and mountains and whatever else.
He has been broken by me many times, breaking all; so I do not fear, divine sage, even an angry wind."
[Narada said:] "Shalmali, your view is mistaken, without doubt; for no being anywhere is equal in strength to the wind.
Indra, Yama, Vaishravana, and Varuna, lord of waters, even they are not equal to the Maruts; what then of you, lord of the forest?
For whatever creature stirs on earth, Shalmali, the blessed wind is everywhere the lord who makes stirring and breath.
He moves creatures rightly when he moves rightly; moving wrongly, he moves again, deformed, among men.
Why do you not honour the wind, such as he is, the best of all who bear beings, the worshipful, through lightness of mind?
You are without substance, ill-minded, and merely talk much; covered with anger and the rest, you speak falsely, Shalmali.
Anger has risen in me as you speak thus; I myself shall tell the wind your many ill words.
Sandalwoods, spandanas, sals, pines, deodars, reeds, and others still stronger,
even they, ill-minded one, have not so insulted the wind, being self-controlled; for they know the strength of the wind and their own.
Therefore those best of trees bow to the wind; but you, through delusion, do not know the endless strength of the wind."
[Narada said to the Wind:] "A certain silk-cotton tree on the Himalaya's flank, with many dependents, with a great root and great branches, despises you, Wind.
He spoke to you many words of insult; they are not fit for me to speak to you, lord.
I know you, Wind, as the best of all who bear breath, the highest and the greatest, in anger like Vaivasvata."
Hearing Narada's words, the wind approached that Shalmali, enraged, and said:

Shalmali, what you said to Narada, reviling me: I am the wind; I shall show you my power, my strength.
mahabharata:12:151.7	I do know you, and you are known to me, tree; Grandfather Brahma rested on you at the creation of beings.
mahabharata:12:151.8	Because of his resting, the favour that was done to you, you are protected by that, ill-minded, lowest of trees, not by your own strength.
mahabharata:12:151.9	Since you despise me as another common thing, I shall show you myself, so that you will know me.
[Shalmali said:] "Give up your anger toward me; what will you do to me in anger? I do not fear you, wind, even if you are lord yourself."
Thus addressed, the wind said, "Tomorrow! I shall show you my strength"; then night came.
Then Shalmali, considering in his mind what the wind had caused, seeing himself unequal to Matarishvan,
thought, "What I said to Narada about the wind was false; I am unable against the wind, for he is mighty by strength.
The wind is ever mighty, as Narada said; I am indeed weaker than other trees, without doubt.
But in intelligence no tree is equal to me; relying on that intelligence I shall be free of the fear of the wind.
If leafy trees in the forest were to act relying on that wisdom, they would always be safe from the angry wind, without doubt.
The foolish ones here do not know it, how the wind, enraged, would not blow upon them; I know how."
Then, resolved in mind and agitated, Shalmali himself shed his branches, trunks and twigs.
Having cast off his branches, leaves and flowers, the tree at dawn looked for the wind's coming.
Then the angry wind, blowing, felling great trees, came to that place where the Shalmali stood.
Seeing him stripped of leaves, with fallen top branches and scattered flowers, the wind spoke smiling to the broken-branched Shalmali, who was joyful.

I too, Shalmali, would have done just this to you in anger: by yourself you have done the whole stripping of the branches.
mahabharata:12:151.24	Stripped of flowers and top branches, with shed shoots and leaves, by your own ill counsel you have come under the power of my strength.
Hearing this speech of the wind, Shalmali was ashamed then, and tormented, remembering what Narada had said.
So, tiger among kings, the weak man who sets enmity with the stronger suffers like a child, as Shalmali did.
Therefore a weak man should not make enmity with the stronger; the one who makes enmity would grieve, as Shalmali did.
The great-souled do not reveal enmity toward those who have wronged them; slowly, slowly, great king, they show their strength.
The ill-minded man should not make enmity with one who lives by intelligence; the intelligence of the intelligent goes like fire in cotton.
There is nothing in a man equal to intelligence, king, nor to strength, lord of kings; let one think that none is equal.
Therefore one should be patient toward the child, the dull and the deaf, and toward the stronger, lord of kings; that was seen in you, slayer of foes.
Eleven akshauhinis, and seven too, resplendent one, were not equal in strength, king, to the great-souled Arjuna.
They were slain and broken by the glorious Pandava, who, relying on strength, roamed the battle, the son of Indra.
The duties of kings and the duties in calamity have been told to you, Bharata, at length, great king; what more shall I say?"
[Bhishma said:] "Hear the seat of sin, lord of men; greed alone is the great crocodile; from greed sin proceeds.
From it come sin and adharma, and the highest sorrow; this is the root of deceit, by which men become doers of sin.
From greed anger arises, from greed desire proceeds; from greed come delusion, deceit, pride, stiffness and murderousness.
Impatience, loss of shame, destruction of fortune, decay of dharma, covetousness and cleverness: all proceed from greed.
Injustice, thoughtlessness, activities in wrong deeds, forgery and the like, and intoxication with beauty and power,
distrust of all beings, crookedness toward all beings, malice toward all beings, unfitness toward all beings, the taking of others' wealth and touching others' wives,
the impulse of speech, the impulse of mind, the impulse of blame, the impulses of the genitals and the belly, and the dreadful impulse of death,
the strong impulse of envy, the hard-to-abandon impulse of falsehood, the impulse of taste that cannot be checked, and the hard-to-bear impulse of hearing.
Greed, which cannot be filled by getting, Kuru's bull, like the ocean ever by deep-watered rivers, one who does not rejoice in gains and is not sated by desires,
which is not truly known by gods, gandharvas, asuras, great serpents or all hosts of beings, king: that greed, with delusion, must be conquered by one who has conquered himself.
Hypocrisy, malice, blame, backbiting and jealousy arise, Kauravya, in the greedy who have not mastered themselves.
The much-learned bear very great scriptures, and are cutters of doubts, yet the dull-witted suffer here.

Attached to hatred and anger, cast out from the conduct of the good, sharp within and sweet outside, like wells covered with grass, petty snarers in the name of dharma, bannerbearers, they rob the world.
They make many paths, relying on the strength of arguments, and wipe out the whole road, settled in greed and ignorance.
The institution of dharma, when it is carried off by the evil-souled seized by greed, whatever is altered, thereby it is entered.
Pride, anger, intoxication, sleep, joy, grief and excessive self-regard are seen, Kauravya, in greedy minds; know these as the unrefined, ever joined with greed.
But ask the refined, of pure vows, whom I shall name, in whom there is no fear for livelihood, nor fear of the next world.
They have no attachment to meat, nor to the pleasant or unpleasant; they love the conduct of the good and are established in self-control.
To them pleasure and pain are the highest; truth is their refuge; they are givers, not takers, and compassionate.
They honour ancestors, gods and guests, ever diligent, benefactors of all, steadfast, upholders of all dharma.
They are for the good of all beings, and give everything, Bharata; they cannot be moved, having reached the far shore of the work of dharma.
Their conduct, made earlier by the good, is not broken; they are not timid or restless or fierce, but stand on the path of the good.

Those in whom non-violence is established are always to be served by the good; those free of desire and anger, without possessiveness and ego, of good vows and fixed limits: attend on them and question them.
Yudhishthira, their dharma is not for cattle or fame; the actions of the body are done as an unavoidable duty.
In them there is no fear, anger, restlessness, or grief; they are not displayers of dharma, and keep nothing secret.
Be attached, Kaunteya, to those in whom there is no greed or delusion, who delight in truth and honesty, and whose minds are made untiring.
Those who do not rejoice in gains nor suffer in losses, without possessiveness or ego, established in sattva, seeing all alike,
for whom gain and loss, pleasure and pain, dear and undear, death and life are alike, of steady valour, whose selves are awakened, abiding in goodness,
those of great might, who love not pleasure, you should serve with effort and without heedlessness. By fate all become virtuous, as with good and bad speech and lamentation alike."
[Bhishma said:] "He who does sin out of ignorance and does not know what is fit for himself, and hates those of good conduct, comes to be spoken ill of by the world.
By ignorance one goes to hell, by ignorance to a bad end; by ignorance one meets affliction and sinks in calamities."
[Yudhishthira said:] "The origin of ignorance, its seat, growth, rise and decay, its root, its yoga, its course, its time, cause and reason,
I wish to hear in truth, as it is, here, lord of the earth; for this sorrow that is found here arises from ignorance."
[Bhishma said:] "Attachment, aversion, delusion, joy, grief, pride, desire, anger, arrogance, drowsiness and sloth,
wish, hatred, heat, increase and torment: this is declared to be ignorance, and the actions that are sinful.
The course arising from it, and the growth and the rest that you ask about, hear in detail, mighty-armed, lord of the people.
These two, ignorance and excessive greed, are equal in fruit and equal in fault, Bharata; know them as one, lord of the earth.
The root of great greed is time, whose nature is its course; whether greed is cut or not cut, time alone is the cause.
From ignorance of it comes greed, and from greed ignorance; all faults come from greed; therefore one should avoid greed.
Janaka, Yuvanashva, Vrishadarbhi, Prasenajit, and other lords of men reached heaven through the destruction of greed.
But, best of the Kurus, visibly, abandon greed here yourself; having abandoned greed, you will go happily in this world and the next."
[Yudhishthira said:] "In the many views of the world, tell me what you hold to be the highest good here, in this world and the next, grandsire.
This path of dharma is great and many-branched, Bharata; which of the dharmas is held to be the most fit to be practised?
Of the great dharma of many branches, king, what is the highest root in truth, dear? Tell me all, untiring."
[Bhishma said:] "Well, I shall tell you that by which you will attain the highest good; as if drinking nectar, the wise one will be sated with knowledge.
The rules of dharma are many, each declared by the great sages according to their own knowledge; but self-control is the refuge of them all."
[Yudhishthira said:] "By what householder, relying on dharma, was death conquered? Tell me all this in truth, king."
Equal in strength to ten thousand elephants, like a second Vishnu himself, that righteous-souled one, about to sacrifice, had thousands of shining vessels made of gold.
Permitted by you, hero, I shall resort to the forests, wearing bark and rags, king, together with this Gandhari, and as a forest-dweller I shall utter blessings upon you.
As Shaineya was being slain, the son of Rukmini, enraged, rushed in between to save the son of Shini.
[Vaishampayana said:] Hearing that speech of the king of dharma, the blessed one in the form of Dharma, intent on Yudhishthira, spoke to the lord of men with gentle words filled with praise.
When those bright-bodied beings, of holy birth and deeds, had come together, the gods, that darkness departed, king.
